title: How Britain Can Help Build a Fairer Global Economy
gist: Danny Sriskandarajah argues that with the UK set to hold the G20 presidency in 2027 and the G7 presidency in 2028, new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has a rare opening to champion a new internationalism centered on a fairer global economy — pushing debt relief, curbs on illicit finance, taxes on billionaires and polluters, and reformed aid architecture — provided he abandons his predecessor's defensive posture.

insights.claim: New UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham inherits a foreign policy that feels defensive and diminished after a tumultuous decade bookended by the 2016 Brexit vote and Keir Starmer's premiership, focused on holding fragile alliances together and cutting foreign-aid budgets dramatically under the banner of 'progressive realism.'
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Sets the political baseline against which any shift in UK international economic policy will be measured — a defensive, aid-cutting posture the author wants reversed.
insights.quote: Burnham therefore inherits a foreign policy that feels both defensive and diminished, focused on holding fragile alliances together and cutting foreign-aid budgets dramatically in the name of “progressive realism”—a tagline that inspires no one.
insights.locator: Burnham took over after a tumultuous decade

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah urges Burnham to reject the 'safe option' of keeping Britain's head down and flattering a difficult US president, arguing that launching something new even without full consensus is the better path.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Signals appetite among reform-minded voices for the UK to challenge, rather than accommodate, US economic unilateralism — a potential source of transatlantic friction.
insights.quote: The safe option is to keep Britain’s head down, flatter a difficult US president, and avoid controversy. But defensiveness will not deliver meaningful results.

insights.claim: The UK will hold the G20 presidency in 2027 and the G7 presidency in 2028, a rare back-to-back platform Sriskandarajah says Burnham should seize to shape lasting norms and institutions rather than merely manage threats.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete 2027–2028 agenda-setting window in which the UK could push global economic-governance reforms — a calendar to watch for policy initiatives on debt, tax, and finance.
insights.quote: the UK will hold the G20 presidency in 2027 and the G7 presidency in 2028. Such opportunities are rare; those who seize on them benefit.

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah cites Gordon Brown's role in steadying the world economy in 2009 and Tony Blair's use of the 2005 G8 to advance debt relief and aid for Africa as models of bold British leadership through summit diplomacy.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that UK summit presidencies have moved global outcomes before — a benchmark for gauging whether the 2027–2028 presidencies deliver substance.
insights.quote: Many still recall how Prime Minister Gordon Brown helped steady the world economy in 2009, and how his predecessor, Tony Blair, used the 2005 G8 to advance debt relief and aid for Africa.

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah proposes the UK could urge concrete action on the debt crises 'strangling dozens of countries,' crack down on illicit financial flows, or introduce a minimum tax on billionaires to signal it wants to shape the future rather than salvage the past.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Names specific policy levers — sovereign debt relief, anti-illicit-finance measures, billionaire taxation — that could gain momentum on the UK-led G20/G7 agenda, with implications for EM debt and wealth taxation.
insights.quote: Britain, for its part, could urge concrete action on the debt crises that are strangling dozens of countries, crack down on illicit financial flows, or introduce a minimum tax on billionaires.
insights.locator: Britain, for its part, could urge

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah points to South Africa launching the International Panel on Inequality during its G20 presidency and Brazil putting taxation of the super-rich into its Rio leaders' declaration as precedents for launching initiatives without full consensus.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Shows the super-rich taxation and inequality agenda is already advancing through G20 presidencies — a direction-of-travel signal for global wealth-tax and inequality policy.
insights.quote: That is what South Africa did with the International Panel on Inequality during its G20 presidency, and it is what Brazil did by putting taxation of the super-rich in its Rio leaders’ declaration.
insights.locator: Launching something new, even without a full consensus

themes.theme: Coalitions of the willing and solidarity levies

insights.claim: Barbados, France, and Kenya are co-chairing a Global Solidarity Levies Task Force to develop new international fees on aviation, premium flyers, shipping, fossil-fuel extraction, and financial transactions to raise revenue for climate and development finance.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: A concrete multilateral effort to tax aviation, shipping, fossil extraction, and financial transactions — a potential cost input for those sectors and a new development-finance revenue stream to track.
insights.quote: Barbados, France, and Kenya are co-chairing a Global Solidarity Levies Task Force to develop new international fees on aviation, premium flyers, shipping, fossil-fuel extraction, and financial transactions
insights.locator: A good place to start is with the “coalitions of the willing”

insights.claim: Colombia and the Netherlands have led an effort to drive progress on the transition away from fossil fuels, while other 'coalitions of the willing' are working on debt relief, central-bank swap lines, and wealth taxes.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Small-group state coalitions are already advancing fossil-fuel transition, debt relief, swap lines, and wealth taxes without global consensus — an under-tracked channel for policy that could reshape sector and sovereign risk.
insights.quote: Colombia and the Netherlands have led an effort to drive progress on the transition away from fossil fuels, and other groupings are working on debt relief, central-bank swap lines, and wealth taxes

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah argues that letting small groups of countries test novel approaches like pollution-linked solidarity levies — without needing global consensus or overcoming vetoes from powerful states — is how a new 21st-century internationalism is being assembled.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: A framework for how policy now advances — minilateral pilots that scale as more countries join — meaning investors should watch small coalitions, not just the UN or G20, as leading indicators of new global rules.
insights.quote: new initiatives allow a small group of countries to test and study novel approaches without having to achieve a global consensus or overcome vetoes from powerful countries
insights.locator: In some cases, like the proposal to tax polluting activities

insights.claim: Sriskandarajah argues the world still relies on aid architecture designed by a 1960s commission, based on an outdated donor-recipient model, even though aid now accounts for only a small share of the money flowing to the Global South.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Signals that traditional aid is a shrinking piece of development finance, shifting the relevant flows toward levies, private capital, and debt mechanisms — a structural reframing of how the Global South is financed.
insights.quote: Aid now accounts for only a small share of the money flowing to the Global South, and it is based on an outdated donor-recipient model.
insights.locator: Reforms are especially needed in international development

insights.claim: Rather than restoring the symbolic 0.7%-of-GNI aid target, Sriskandarajah says Burnham should commission an independent inquiry into what might replace the aid system altogether, built on universality and solidarity rather than charity.
insights.speaker: DANNY SRISKANDARAJAH
insights.so_what: Points to a possible UK-led rethink of the entire development-finance model, away from aid targets toward solidarity-based mechanisms — a policy direction with long-run implications for how development capital is raised.
insights.quote: Instead, Burnham should commission an independent inquiry into what might replace the system altogether, and to test new ideas built on universality and solidarity rather than charity.
insights.locator: Promising to restore an aid target of 0.7%
